extracted.intended_audience: Congressional staff, patent policymakers, patent practitioners, industry stakeholders, and inventors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for assessing proposed patent-reform provisions (damages, post-grant review, venue, interlocutory appeals, examination policy) and for designing reforms that preserve patent certainty while addressing abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of economic analysis for high-value damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor estimates of damages that are based on economic analysis, rather than the usual shorthand of total product value multiplied by an expert’s unverifiable assertions about what constitutes a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic analyses are expensive, but when tens of millions of dollars are at stake it is appropriate to favor the best available evidence of what a patent is worth rather than simplistic multiplications of product value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relitigation of validity during damages ('specific contribution over the prior art')
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase “specific contribution over the prior art” appears designed to allow de facto relitigation of claim construction and validity issues during the damages phase; validity questions (why the patent was allowed, novelty, nonobviousness) should not be relitigated at damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues of novelty/nonobviousness are validity issues and should be resolved in their proper phase (and if standards need modification, Congress should amend 102, 103, and 112—not section 284). Allowing relitigation overlays a second set of validity standards at damages and undermines bifurcated trial structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit revival of 'gist of the patent' tests that broaden claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests like the “gist of the patent” (used historically under doctrine of equivalents) were discarded because they tended to unduly broaden patent scope and allow plaintiffs to assert rights beyond the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation should not reintroduce vague, overarching tests (e.g., 'gist' or 'nub') that permit plaintiffs to reduce claims to an amorphous core and thereby claim rights outside the actual claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-window (post-grant) review must be inexpensive and substitute for litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening a second window for administrative challenges only makes sense if defending patents in such proceedings is not unduly expensive, and if such proceedings substitute for a phase of district-court litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If second-window proceedings are expensive, they enable harassment of small patentees; they should be structured to be cost-effective and to replace, not merely delay, corresponding litigation phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit discovery and make estoppel rules certain in second-window proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: If second-window proceedings are permitted, they should generally serve as a complete substitute for at least some phase of litigation, include limited discovery, and have clearer estoppel rules than the current 'could have raised' test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estoppel should not be so liberal as to encourage sequential gaming (raising only some prior-art issues, staying litigation, then later raising others). Consider requiring defendants who use the second window to raise all claims of a particular type identified by a reasonable search request to a commercial search firm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory appeals limited to sufficient-record cases and subject to appellate discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Interlocutory appeals should be allowed only if the district court finds there is a sufficient evidentiary record and that an appeal would save judicial resources; the Federal Circuit should retain limited discretion to refuse such appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a district court certifies an interlocutory appeal on a manifestly inadequate record, the Federal Circuit should be permitted to reject the certification and refuse the appeal when the district court’s predicate findings are clearly erroneous to avoid premature, possibly incorrect final claim construction rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mandate prior-art subtraction in every damages case
rubrics_metrics.description: A requirement of prior-art subtraction in every case is objectionable because many reasonable-royalty measures (established royalties, design-around costs, noninfringing alternatives, cost savings) already deduct the value of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandating prior-art subtraction universally risks double-counting deductions and undervaluing the patented invention; damages law must remain flexible to account for diverse factual scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unsound damages valuation heuristics and weak comparables
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuation methods such as the 'rule of thumb' (e.g., 40% of profits), using the industry average license as a starting point, an IBM-attributed '1% of revenues' rule, and uncritical reliance on comparables are unsound and subject to manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages methods should not rely on such heuristics or improperly justified comparables; courts and legislatures should discourage mechanical formulas that produce inflated or unreliable awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve flexibility in damages (Georgia-Pacific factors) and avoid de facto compulsory licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: The fifteen Georgia-Pacific factors preserve flexibility for jury calculations across varied business circumstances; mandatory apportionment or blanket rules could create de facto compulsory licensing insufficiently compensatory to patentees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifting to rigid mandatory apportionment risks under-compensating patent holders and making infringement a cost-of-doing-business rather than a deterrent; consider codifying balanced factors rather than imposing draconian bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue reforms should not unduly restrict plaintiffs' forum choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Venue provisions that sweep too broadly in favor of defendants unduly restrict plaintiffs' choice of forum and may deter legitimate infringement suits, even when narrow carve-outs exist for universities and nonprofits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation addressing forum-shopping should strike a balance — prevent abusive forum-shopping without denying plaintiffs reasonable access to favorable forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant opposition must be timely, streamlined, safeguarded, and manageable for USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: A post-grant opposition system should serve to solidify validity or catch patents that should have been rejected, be timely and streamlined, and provide cost-effective alternatives to litigation while including safeguards to protect patent owners from unwarranted, duplicative, or abusive challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the system so it does not overwhelm USPTO resources or substitute for full litigation piecemeal; study foreign experiences (EU, Japan, Korea, China, Taiwan) where post-grant systems created opportunities for harassment and were revised or scrapped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer improving pre-grant examination over broad post-grant revocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than launching a broad second-window post-grant review, Congress should put more energy into making pre-grant examination more rigorous and improving access to prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strengthening USPTO examination (more examiners, training, resources, access to prior art) reduces 'junk patent' issuance without destabilizing patent rights by subjecting patents to perpetual post-issuance uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen USPTO resources and permanently end fee diversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Improving patent quality is best achieved by enhancing USPTO examination resources and capabilities, including hiring more examiners, instituting training programs, and committing to performance benchmarks; permanently ending fee diversion will provide predictable funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress should support USPTO capacity-building rather than shifting burdens to post-grant mechanisms that risk uncertainty and increased litigation costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise caution in legislation given recent Supreme Court/Federal Circuit decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent decisions (eBay, KSR, MedImmune, In re Seagate) have significantly altered injunction standards, obviousness tests, licensee declaratory judgment rights, and willfulness standards; Congress should carefully assess these developments before enacting sweeping reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because courts are already reshaping patent law, Congress should scrutinize the combined impact of judicial decisions and new statutes to avoid unnecessary or harmful duplication of change.
